hook: A prince who gave up his palace to find the end of suffering, and woke up.

pages.x: Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, a prince of the Shakya people. Tradition says a wise man foretold he would be either a great king or a great holy man, so his father kept him inside the palace walls, surrounded by every pleasure, and married him young.

At 29, riding outside the palace, he saw an old man, a sick man and a dead body, and learned that everyone grows old, falls ill and dies. Then he saw a calm wandering holy man. That night he left his wife, his baby son and his palace to search for a way to end suffering.

For six years he lived as a hermit, starving himself until, the stories say, he could feel his spine through his stomach. Then he decided that punishing the body was as useless as spoiling it. He accepted a bowl of rice and milk from a village girl, and chose a Middle Way.

At Bodh Gaya he sat under a fig tree and vowed not to get up until he understood. Legend says the demon Mara sent armies and temptations; he touched the earth to be his witness. At dawn he became the Buddha, "the one who woke up". The temple there is the holiest place in Buddhism.

In a deer park at Sarnath he gave his first teaching: life brings suffering; suffering comes from craving; it can end; and the Eightfold Path of right understanding, speech, action and mindfulness leads there. For 45 years he taught across northern India, to kings and outcasts, men and women.

At about 80, at Kushinagar, he fell ill after a meal and lay down between two trees. His last words to his followers were: "All things that are made will pass away. Strive on with care." Buddhists call his death the parinirvana, the final release.

The Buddha's teachings spread from India to Sri Lanka, China, Korea, Japan, Tibet and Southeast Asia. Today around 500 million people are Buddhists, and his ideas on mindfulness and compassion reach millions more.
